13:7.text: And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.

provenance.other: “Glad tidings” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Luke 1:19, Luke 8:1, Acts 13:32, Romans 10:15), of which Luke 1:19 is the only one where an angel brings them and the only one that couples them with being sent.
provenance.significance: Samuel's credentials are Gabriel's. The angel of Luke 1 answers a doubting priest by naming himself, saying he was sent, and saying what he was sent with — glad tidings; Samuel, standing on a wall over a city that has already thrown him out, says the same three things in the same order. The suppressed correspondence is the reception: Gabriel strikes Zacharias dumb for not believing, and Samuel's hearers will spend chapter 16 shooting arrows at him. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the borrowed frame carries its own outcome with it.

13:7.note: 'An angel of the Lord hath declared it unto me, and he did bring glad tidings to my soul. And behold, I was sent unto you to declare it unto you also, that ye might have glad tidings.' Against Luke 1:19: 'I am Gabriel … and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.' The three elements — angel, sent, glad tidings — are Luke's, and 'glad tidings' occurs in exactly four KJV verses of which this is the only angelic one. The Book of Mormon then does something Luke does not: it makes the prophet a relay, receiving the tidings and passing them on in the same words. Note that the immediately following verse borrows from two verses earlier in the same speech (13:8, Luke 1:17), which is the sequence argument for reading this as Luke 1 rather than the general KJV idiom.

13:8.text: And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

provenance.route: Malachi 4:6 → Luke 1:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Turn the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:17. Malachi 4:6, which Luke is quoting, has the singular — 'turn the heart of the fathers to the children' — and so does 3 Nephi 25:6 when the Book of Mormon transcribes Malachi outright.
provenance.significance: The Elijah promise, run backwards. In Malachi and in Luke, turning hearts is the last mercy before the curse; here the Lord turns hearts as the curse. Recover the source and the threat has a shape the verse does not state: what is withdrawn from the Nephites is not merely favour but the specific eleventh-hour reconciliation Malachi ends the Old Testament by promising, and the hearts turned are their brethren's — the Lamanites', the very people Samuel belongs to and chapter 15 will say the Lord has kept.

13:8.note: 'I will turn the hearts of their brethren against them.' The plural 'turn the hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:17, Gabriel's citation of Malachi's Elijah promise; Malachi 4:6 itself reads 'turn the heart' in the singular. The Book of Mormon has Luke's plural, which is a small mediation result and not a decisive one — the phrase is short and the sense is inverted from reconciliation to estrangement. What carries it is the company: the previous verse borrows Luke 1:19, two verses further on in Gabriel's same speech. Recorded at moderate because the inversion is deliberate enough to be an argument and thin enough to be denied.
13:8.whyNot: Three words, and the sense is opposed to both Malachi's and Luke's. A reader who takes 'turn the hearts of X against Y' as ordinary English prophetic idiom rather than a citation is not being unreasonable; the case rests on the plural and on 13:7.

13:9.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.

provenance.other: The triad in the order sword–famine–pestilence is Jeremiah's signature; “the sword the famine and the pestilence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 24:10 and Jeremiah 29:17, both with a single article. Jeremiah 14:12 repeats the preposition — 'by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence' — which is the construction the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: Samuel is preaching in the seventh-century idiom of the prophet whose city fell. Jeremiah 14 is the drought oracle in which the Lord forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people; the Book of Mormon puts its judgment formula in the mouth of a prophet who has just been told to go back and preach to a people he had given up on — the opposite instruction, in the same words.

13:9.note: 'I will visit them with the sword, and with famine, and with pestilence.' The triad is Jeremiah's and the repeated preposition points at Jeremiah 14:12 ('by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence') rather than the single-article form of Jeremiah 24:10 and 29:17. Ezekiel has the same three judgments but almost always with a fourth, the noisome beast (Ezekiel 14:21), and Leviticus 26 keeps them separate. Moderate because the formula is distributed across a dozen Jeremiah verses and no single one can be isolated — the finding is the idiom, not the verse.

13:10.text: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;

provenance.other: “Unto the third and fourth generation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Exodus 20:5, Exodus 34:7 and Deuteronomy 5:9 — and Numbers 14:18 has the same formula with 'unto the third and fourth'. All four pair the span with the verb 'visiting'. The bare phrase 'fourth generation' is commoner, seven verses, the other three being Genesis 15:16, 2 Kings 10:30 and 2 Kings 15:12.
provenance.significance: The second commandment supplies both the verb and the arithmetic, and the Book of Mormon turns the sanction inside out. In Exodus the Lord visits iniquity on the children to the fourth generation; here the fourth generation is the audience rather than the object — they survive to watch, and then 'shall visit your destruction'. The visiting passes from God to the enemy, which is what makes the borrowing worth recording: the commandment's clause is not being quoted, it is being cashed.

13:10.note: 'I will visit them in my fierce anger, and there shall be those of the fourth generation … to behold your utter destruction … and those of the fourth generation shall visit your destruction.' “Unto the third and fourth generation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them the Decalogue's jealous-God clause. Both terms of that sanction are here — the verb 'visit' and the span 'fourth generation' — and no other KJV context puts them together. Moderate rather than high because the shared wording is two elements rather than a clause, and because 'fourth generation' has three unrelated KJV homes (Genesis 15:16, 2 Kings 10:30, 2 Kings 15:12).

13:13.text: And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.

provenance.other: “Spare all the place” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 18:26, and it is the only KJV sentence in which a city is spared on account of the righteous inside it. “Fire come down from heaven” occurs in three (2 Kings 1:10, 1:12, Revelation 13:13) and none of those is a city; Genesis 19:24 has the Sodom fire but calls it 'brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven'.
provenance.significance: Abraham's bargain, with the arithmetic dropped and the outcome kept. Genesis 18 works by counting — fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten — and the reader who recovers it knows how the story ends: the number could not be found and the fire fell anyway. Samuel's next sentence supplies exactly that ending in advance ('when ye shall cast out the righteous from among you, then shall ye be ripe for destruction'), so the metalepsis is doing the argument's work. Zarahemla is being told it is Sodom on the night before, and that the count is going down.

13:13.note: 'If it were not for the righteous which are in this great city, behold I would cause that fire should come down out of heaven, and destroy it.' The proposition is Genesis 18:26's: a city spared for the righteous in it, and burned otherwise. 'Spare all the place' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The fire is Sodom's from the next chapter (Genesis 19:24), and 13:14's 'it is for the righteous' sake, that it is spared' reproduces Genesis 18:26's 'for their sakes'. Note that 2 Kings 1:10, the machine's likelier match on the fire clause alone, has no city and no righteous remnant, and is filed in the register.

13:19.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

provenance.other: “Treasures upon earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:19. The Sermon's antithesis — treasure laid up on earth against treasure laid up with God — has no Old Testament equivalent.
provenance.significance: The Sermon on the Mount's antithesis made literal and local. Matthew's earthly treasure is lost to moth, rust and thieves; Samuel's is lost to the ground itself, which becomes slippery and will not hold it. The metalepsis is in what Matthew's 'treasures in heaven' becomes here: not a heavenly deposit but 'hide up their treasures unto me' — the same act of burying, redirected. The consolation is that the Lord is the only bank in a cursed land.

13:19.note: 13:18-19 sets 'whoso shall hide up treasures in the earth, shall find them again no more' against 'they shall hide up their treasures unto me', which is the structure of Matthew 6:19-20 with the verb changed from laying up to hiding up. 'Treasures upon earth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate rather than high: the shared material is the antithesis and the noun, not a clause, and the hiding of treasure in the earth is also the servant's act in Matthew 25:18. The heart clause that completes the Sermon's argument arrives one verse later and is adjudicated at 13:20.

13:20.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.other: “Set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 62:10, and it is the only KJV sentence that attaches the setting of the heart to riches specifically. Matthew 6:21's 'there will your heart be' occurs in exactly two, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34.
provenance.significance: The psalm's prohibition is quoted as an indictment: what Psalm 62 tells the hearer not to do is what Samuel says the hearer has done. Recovering the psalm supplies the reason the Book of Mormon does not give — Psalm 62:9 has just weighed men in the balance and found them 'altogether lighter than vanity', so the riches that are about to become slippery were already weightless.

13:20.note: 'Because they have set their hearts upon riches … because they have set their hearts upon their riches.' Psalm 62:10's 'if riches increase, set not your heart upon them' is the only KJV verse joining those two ideas, and the phrase 'set not your heart upon' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 6:21 supplies the treasure-and-heart form the previous verse was already using, so the two sources are working together rather than competing. Moderate: 'set the heart upon' is idiomatic enough that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without the psalm in view.

13:22.text: For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:

provenance.other: “Swellings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:20, which also carries 'envyings' (two KJV verses, this and Galatians 5:21) and 'strifes' (four). No other KJV verse has any two of the three together.
provenance.significance: Paul's list is what he fears to find when he arrives; Samuel's is what he says is already there. The suppressed correspondence is that 2 Corinthians 12:20-21 is written by an apostle who expects to be humbled by the congregation he is coming to — and the man on the wall is delivering the same catalogue to a city that has already thrown him over it.

13:22.note: 'They do swell with great pride, unto boasting, and unto great swelling, envyings, strifes, malice, persecutions, and murders.' Three of the vices — swelling, envyings, strifes — are the distinctive ones, and the single KJV verse that carries all three is 2 Corinthians 12:20; 'swellings' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Great swelling' as a phrase belongs to 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 16, where it describes the speech of false teachers, which is the subject of 13:27-28 five verses later. Galatians 5:20-21 supplies 'murders' next to 'envyings' but has neither swelling nor strife in the plural.

13:22.text: But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.

provenance.other: “Power to get wealth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:18, which is also one of only two KJV verses reading “remember the LORD thy God” (the other, 2 Samuel 14:11, is the woman of Tekoah's oath).
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8 is the chapter that anticipates prosperity and legislates against forgetting; Samuel reports the failure the chapter was written to forestall, in the chapter's own sequence — forget who gave it (8:11-14), heart lifted up (8:14), the wealth was his to give (8:18). What the borrowing adds is the verdict: Moses says 'lest thou forget', and the Book of Mormon says the lest has happened.

13:22.note: 'Ye do not remember the Lord your God in the things which he hath blessed you … hath not hearkened unto the words of him who gave them unto you' (13:21-22). Deuteronomy 8:18 is the KJV's one verse on God as the giver of the power to get wealth, and Deuteronomy 8:14's 'then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God' is the sentence the Book of Mormon's 'they do swell with great pride' translates into its own idiom. Moderate: the contact is a sustained sequence of ideas with one rare phrase behind it rather than a reproduced clause.

13:25.text: And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.
variants: 1830 'ye would not have slain' → 1920 'we would not have slain'

provenance.other: “In the days of our fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:30. Luke's version of the same woe (Luke 11:47-48) has no counterfactual at all — it reads 'ye allow the deeds of your fathers' — so Matthew is the only possible source for the sentence's shape as well as its words.
provenance.significance: This is the hinge of the whole sermon, and the metalepsis runs forward rather than back. In Matthew the woe is an argument in three moves: you say you would not have killed the prophets (23:30), therefore you witness against yourselves that you are their children (23:31), and Jerusalem's house is left desolate (23:38). Samuel makes all three moves in the same order across two chapters — the disclaimer here, 'ye are worse than they' at 13:26, and 'your houses shall be left unto you desolate' at 15:1. Recovering Matthew tells the reader what Zarahemla is being cast as before the sermon says it: Jerusalem in the last week.

13:25.note: 'If our days had been in the days of our fathers of old, ye would not have slain the prophets; ye would not have stoned them, and cast them out.' Matthew 23:30: 'If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.' The conditional, the phrase 'in the days of our fathers' — a KJV singleton — and the disavowal are all reproduced; what the Book of Mormon substitutes for Matthew's 'partakers … in the blood' is 'slain the prophets … stoned them', which is Matthew 23:37's 'thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them' seven verses further on. So the verse fuses the two ends of the same woe. The 1830 reading is evidence here: the first edition has 'YE would not have slain', which is incoherent inside a speech the people are quoting of themselves, and 1920 changed it to 'we' — that is, the later edition corrected the text back toward the KJV's pronoun (CONVENTIONS §8). Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

13:28.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “Flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The KJV's other flattery language is Psalmic and uses 'lips', 'mouth' or 'tongue' (Psalm 5:9, 12:2-3, Proverbs 26:28, 29:5).
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a denial and Samuel's is an accusation, and they name the same two things in the same order. 1 Thessalonians 2:5 disclaims flattering words and 'a cloke of covetousness'; Helaman 13:28 has the flattering words and then the gold, the silver and the costly apparel that are the covetousness the cloak is for. Recovering Paul gives the verse a control it does not state: this is what a true preacher is on record as not doing, and 13:26 has just said what happens to one who does not do it.

13:28.note: 'Because he speaketh flattering words unto you, and he saith that all is well.' 'Flattering words' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is Paul distinguishing himself from precisely the paid flatterer Samuel describes. The surrounding detail — substance, gold, silver, costly apparel — matches Paul's 'cloke of covetousness' rather than the psalms' flattering lips. Moderate: two words, and the Book of Mormon uses 'flattering words' as a settled formula elsewhere in its own text, so this may be its idiom rather than a fresh borrowing here.

13:29.text: Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!

provenance.other: “Blind guides” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:16 and Matthew 23:24, both inside the same discourse the sermon has already quoted at 13:25. Luke's parallel woes have 'ye are as graves which appear not' (Luke 11:44) and no guides at all.
provenance.significance: The confirmation of the Matthew 23 reading, four verses after the quotation that established it. A single borrowing from a discourse can be an accident of memory; two, from verses fourteen apart in one chapter, with the epithet reserved to that chapter in the whole King James Bible, is a sustained use. And the epithet is chosen for its object: Matthew's blind guides are the religious leadership, and Samuel is telling a people that the leaders they have chosen over him are that.

13:29.note: 'How long will ye suffer yourselves to be lead by foolish and blind guides?' 'Blind guides' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both are Matthew 23, the discourse already quoted at 13:25. The Book of Mormon adds 'foolish', which is not Matthew's, and turns the epithet from an address ('ye blind guides') into a description of the people the audience follows — the same move it makes with the woes themselves. 1830 reads 'lead' where 1920 reads 'led'.

13:29.text: Then Jesus answered and said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him hither to me.

provenance.other: “Perverse generation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:17 and Luke 9:41, and the doubled question “how long shall I suffer you” in exactly two, Matthew 17:17 and Mark 9:19. Luke 9:41 collapses the two questions into one ('how long shall I be with you, and suffer you?'), so the anaphora is Matthew's and Mark's, not Luke's.
provenance.significance: The address is Christ's to his own disciples' generation at the foot of the mount of transfiguration; Samuel gives it to a city. The suppressed half is what follows in Matthew — the failure being rebuked there is a failure of faith to cast out a devil, and Samuel's next chapters are about signs given so that 'there should be no cause for unbelief'.

13:29.note: 'O ye wicked and ye perverse generation … how long will ye suppose that the Lord will suffer you? Yea, how long will ye suffer yourselves …? Yea, how long will ye choose darkness …?' The epithet and the anaphora both come from one KJV sentence: 'perverse generation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and 'how long shall I suffer you' in exactly two, with Matthew 17:17 the only verse in both lists. The Book of Mormon extends the doubled 'how long' to three and puts the suffering in the audience's mouth as well as God's, which is a rhetorical development of the source rather than a repetition of it.

13:29.text: And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.

provenance.other: “Darkness rather than light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:19, and the clause that completes it there — 'because their deeds were evil' — has already been used three verses earlier at Helaman 13:26 ('because he testifieth that your deeds are evil').
provenance.significance: Split agreement across three verses, which is exactly what the contiguous-window machine stream cannot see (CONVENTIONS §9). John 3:19 is one sentence with two halves; the Book of Mormon uses the second half at 13:26 and the first half at 13:29, in reverse order, and both halves keep their function — the deeds are why the prophet is hated, and the darkness is what the hearers choose. John 3:20 supplies the missing middle term the Book of Mormon does not state: 'every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved.' That is a description of 13:26's audience.

13:29.note: 'How long will ye choose darkness rather than light?' 'Darkness rather than light' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What raises this above a stock antithesis is that 13:26 has already used the other half of the same Johannine sentence — the prophet is cast out 'because he testifieth that your deeds are evil', against John 3:19's 'because their deeds were evil'. The Book of Mormon's one addition is the verb: John's men loved darkness, Samuel's choose it, which is the freedom argument chapter 14 will end on (14:31, 'ye might choose life or death').

13:31.text: Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction.

provenance.other: “Slippery” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 35:6, Psalm 73:18 and Jeremiah 23:12. Only Psalm 73:18 is about the prosperous, and only it pairs slipperiness with destruction ('thou castedst them down into destruction').
provenance.significance: Psalm 73 is the KJV's sustained complaint about the wealth of the wicked — 'they have more than heart could wish', 'they increase in riches' — answered by the discovery that the Lord had set them in slippery places all along. Samuel's cursing of riches so that 'it becometh slippery, that ye cannot hold them' takes the psalm's metaphor off the people and puts it on the property. Recover the psalm and the answer to Samuel's audience is already there: the security they think they are losing was never footing.

13:31.note: The Book of Mormon's famous slippery treasures are its own image and are not in the King James Bible; what is there is one psalm in which God sets the rich in slippery places and casts them into destruction. 'Slippery' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and the other two are about the way of the wicked, not their goods. Moderate and offered as an echo: a single adjective, but a rare one used of the same people for the same reason, and the whole complex at 13:31-36 (riches, slipperiness, destruction, and the lament that follows) is Psalm 73's subject in Psalm 73's order.

13:32.text: Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.

provenance.other: “Heaped treasure together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 5:3; so do 'riches are corrupted' (James 5:2) and 'your gold and silver' (James 5:3). “Weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 5:1 and Joel 1:5 — but only James has it as a phrase, Joel reading 'and weep; and howl' across a clause break to a different audience.
provenance.significance: Four KJV singletons from three consecutive verses, and the Book of Mormon has kept James's sequence: the summons to weep and howl, then the wealth itself failing. What recovering James adds is the reason — 'ye have heaped treasure together FOR THE LAST DAYS' — which is precisely what Samuel says the Nephites have done and precisely why the treasure is useless: it was stored against a day that has arrived. James's hoard rusts; Samuel's sinks into the ground. Both are unreachable on the morning the owner needs them, and 13:34's 'our swords are taken from us in the day we have sought them for battle' is that image at its most concrete.

13:32.note: 'And then shall ye weep and howl in that day, saith the Lord of Hosts.' James 5:1 is the KJV's one verse in which the phrase 'weep and howl' stands as a unit, and it is addressed to rich men whose riches are about to fail. The lament Samuel then puts in their mouths at 13:33-35 — 'our riches are gone from us', 'we have hid up our treasures, and they have slipped away' — works through James 5:2-3, each of whose distinctive phrases ('riches are corrupted', 'your gold and silver', 'heaped treasure together') is a KJV singleton. Note that 13:28 has already used James's gold and silver of the false prophet's fee. Joel 1:5 has the summons to weep and to howl in a different construction and to drunkards, and is filed in the register.

13:38.text: (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:8 → 2 Corinthians 6:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Day of salvation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2 — and 2 Corinthians 6:2 is Paul quoting Isaiah 49:8, so the phrase has one home in the KJV and one citation of it. Paul's addition is the urgency: 'behold, NOW is the day of salvation.'
provenance.significance: Samuel's charge is that the day has been let go by, which only makes sense against a text that says the day is now. Recover 2 Corinthians 6:2 and the accusation has a clock in it: Paul's 'now' is what 'procrastinated' negates. Isaiah 49:8 alone would not support the reading, since there the day of salvation is God's and no hearer can miss it by delay.

13:38.note: 'Ye have procrastinated the day of your salvation, until it is everlastingly too late.' 'Day of salvation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and only 2 Corinthians 6:2 turns it into a deadline. Echo rather than allusion because the shared material is a three-word phrase that the Book of Mormon uses as a standing formula elsewhere in its own text; what argues for Paul here is the temporal logic rather than the words.
